items.source: Kurt S. Altrichter / RiskSignal Report (Ivory Hill) — The Millisecond Market
items.title: Four sessions, full emotional cycle: -5.3%, +6.5%, -1.5%, then a 4.6% intraday hole that closed -0.6%
items.idea: Nasdaq fell 5.3% Fri Nov 20 (week -10.0%), spiked 6.51% Mon after Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang (NVDA +30% premarket), fell 1.48% Tue, then was -4.63% by 11:31am Wed before closing at 23,586 (-0.62%). The index is still ~14.5% below its Oct 6 record close of 27,599.89.
items.angle: A single governance headline moved a $5T+ stock 30% premarket. That's a sign of how much of the AI trade sits on one key-person risk, not on fundamentals.
items.tweetA: A boardroom vote added 6.5% to the Nasdaq in one day. Earnings didn't change. Capex didn't change. That's how much of this index is a bet on one person staying in one chair. $NVDA $QQQ
items.tweetB: Wednesday the Nasdaq was down 4.6% by 11:30 and closed -0.6%. Intraday ranges like that usually show up near lows, not in the middle of a trend. Watch whether the 23,000 area holds as a higher low on real volume Monday.

items.source: Kurt S. Altrichter / RiskSignal Report (Ivory Hill) — The Millisecond Market
items.title: Algos are 60-73% of US equity volume, and that's why drawdowns now happen in hours
items.idea: Citing JPM/Bloomberg estimates, algorithmic trading is ~60-73% of US equity volume. Altrichter argues machines price headlines in milliseconds, so drawdowns and V-shaped recoveries compress into days and overnight sessions, and he expects daily swings to get more violent as AI is layered on top.
items.angle: If market structure is compressing the cycle, vol-of-vol should stay structurally higher. That favours owning convexity over static allocations.
items.tweetA: If 70% of volume is machines, a 'correction' is no longer a regime. It's an inventory event. The trade is no longer 'when to get out', it's 'who has dry powder at the 3-day low'.
items.tweetB: Everyone talks about AI eating white-collar jobs. Execution was the first job it took, around 2010. The result: 10% drawdowns that recover before the quarterly committee meets. Your IPS is slower than the market it governs.

items.source: Kurt S. Altrichter / RiskSignal Report (Ivory Hill) — The Millisecond Market
items.title: CTA + vol-control equity exposure is in the bottom 3% of its history, the zone last seen at the 2022 low and the April 2025 low
items.idea: Ivory Hill's positioning model shows systematic (CTA/vol-control) equity exposure at the 3rd percentile of history. It last hit this zone at the 2022 lows and the April 2025 low. Systematic money sells automatically into chop and has to buy back once realised vol falls. The Nasdaq made its first higher low of the selloff on Wednesday.
items.angle: This is the mechanical bull case. A drop in realised vol alone produces a buying bid, with no need for good news. Pair it with Innes's dealer hedge-unwind point below.
items.tweetA: Systematic equity exposure at the 3rd percentile. The last two times were Oct 2022 and April 2025. Both were within days of the low. The bears need realised vol to stay high, because the moment it fades the machines have to buy.
items.tweetB: This selloff is unusual because the forced sellers are already out. CTAs are at 3rd-percentile exposure. What's left is discretionary money deciding whether to sell a 14% drawdown in a market with 25% EPS growth. That's a hard sell.

items.source: Kurt S. Altrichter / RiskSignal Report (Ivory Hill) — The Millisecond Market
items.title: S&P EPS growing 25%+ YoY for a third straight quarter, while the Fed is set to hike in December
items.idea: Altrichter notes S&P 500 earnings grew more than 25% YoY for the third straight quarter. Meanwhile the Iran war has run since February, oil is down nearly 20% in the past month, and a December Fed hike is priced. He attributes the current damage to midterm uncertainty and the Nvidia leadership drama, not to earnings.
items.angle: A hiking cycle alongside 25% earnings growth is not the 2022 setup, where earnings were falling. It looks more like 1994 or 2004.
items.tweetA: Three straight quarters of 25%+ S&P EPS growth, and the Fed is hiking into it. That isn't a recession setup. It's 1994: rates up, multiple down, earnings carry the index. Painful for duration, survivable for equities. $SPY
items.tweetB: Oil is -20% in a month during an active Iran war. Earnings are +25% YoY. The Fed is hiking. Each fact alone tells a different story, and together they say the market is pricing a policy mistake rather than an earnings one.

items.source: Kurt S. Altrichter / RiskSignal Report (Ivory Hill) — The Millisecond Market
items.title: TLT is still down more than 50% from its 2020 high, a case against the boilerplate 60/40
items.idea: Altrichter attacks the 'always hold long duration' default in model portfolios: TLT has fallen more than 50% from its 2020 high, most of it after 2022 hikes. He argues 100-year return assumptions don't reflect how prices move now.
items.angle: With the Fed hiking again in December, the 'bonds hedge equities' assumption is being tested a second time in four years.
items.tweetA: TLT -50% from peak, and the Fed is hiking again. Two tightening cycles in four years have turned 'long duration as a hedge' from a law of nature into a regime bet. $TLT
items.tweetB: The 60/40 was built for a world where inflation shocks were rare. Since 2020, the bond sleeve has had a larger drawdown than most equity bear markets. What's the hedge now: gold, trend, or cash?

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes — Thanksgiving Bounce
items.title: The bounce is a hedge-unwind bid, not institutional buying, and the real test is Monday
items.idea: Innes argues the pre-Thanksgiving reversal and overnight extension were boosted by the unwinding of US equity downside hedges, a mechanical bid as dealers adjusted bearish exposures. He separates this from genuine institutional buying, and says holiday-thin desks make Thursday/Friday a poor read, so Monday is the real test.
items.angle: Put this next to Altrichter's 3rd-percentile CTA reading. Two mechanical tailwinds (dealer hedge unwind and systematic re-leveraging) are lining up. The question is whether discretionary money follows.
items.tweetA: Hedge unwinds produce the fastest rallies and the least reliable ones. Dealers buying back deltas doesn't reflect anyone's view on AI earnings. I want to see Monday's volume before I believe the double bottom.
items.tweetB: Two separate mechanical bids are hitting at once: dealer put-hedge unwinds (Innes) and CTAs at 3rd-percentile exposure (Altrichter). Neither depends on conviction. If discretionary money stays out, it's a squeeze, not a bottom.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes — Thanksgiving Bounce
items.title: Seoul's plunge-protection playbook: buyback limits eased, short-selling crackdown, ₩23T of shorting in 3 weeks
items.idea: Korea temporarily eased daily corporate share-buyback limits for three months from Nov 24 and launched an intensified crackdown on illegal short selling. It stopped short of a ban or direct state equity purchases. Short-selling turnover hit ~₩23T between Nov 2-20, with foreigners more than 75% of it.
items.angle: Korea is the purest AI-memory beta (Hynix, Samsung). When the government steps in, a shorting ban becomes the next tail, as in 2008, 2011, 2020 and 2023.
items.tweetA: Korea has banned short selling four times since 2008. Shorts did ₩23T in 18 days, 75% of it foreign, and Seoul has already eased buyback caps. If the AI selloff resumes, the ban is next. Not a great setup for anyone short Hynix. $EWY
items.tweetB: Korean regulators' answer to a foreign-led AI short: let companies buy back more of their own stock. Corporate balance sheets become the plunge-protection team. Worth asking who is the marginal buyer of Korean memory names next quarter.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes — Thanksgiving Bounce
items.title: Asia leads the Thanksgiving relay: SK Hynix and Kioxia outperform, Korea/Taiwan tech +2%
items.idea: Stoxx 600 rallied 1.7%. MSCI Asia Pacific rose 0.8%, only its second advance in eleven sessions. SK Hynix and Kioxia outperformed, Taiwan and Korea tech benchmarks rose more than 2%, and European tech gained more than 2%. S&P and NDX futures were up ~0.5%.
items.angle: Memory led the bounce. If the bounce holds, the most-beaten AI segment snaps back hardest, but compare that with the GPU rental and credit data in the Rewiring piece.
items.tweetA: Memory led the bounce: Hynix and Kioxia beat everything else in Asia. Memory fell first in the AI selloff and is bouncing first. Watch whether HBM pricing holds, because that decides whether this is a bounce or a turn. $MU
items.tweetB: MSCI Asia Pacific was up for only the 2nd time in 11 sessions. Two up days don't make a trend, but Korea had to change its market rules to get this one.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes — Thanksgiving Bounce
items.title: Cross-asset confirmation: copper off an 11-month low, Brent back above $96, EGBs sold
items.idea: Copper recovered nearly 1% from an 11-month low, Brent rose above $96 for the first time in more than a week, and European government bonds weakened as haven demand eased. Innes reads cyclicals and commodities joining as making the rebound more credible, while warning one holiday session proves little.
items.angle: Brent at $96 sits awkwardly next to Altrichter's 'oil down ~20% in the past month'. Either way, the market has crude in the mid-90s during an active Iran war.
items.tweetA: Brent is above $96 again and copper is off an 11-month low on the same day. That's what a growth scare looks like when it fades. If both hold into Monday, the risk-on case is about more than semis.
items.tweetB: Odd pairing: copper at an 11-month low and Brent in the mid-$90s. Industrial demand is weak and energy is supply-constrained, which is a stagflation mix, not a soft landing. Which one does the Fed respond to in December?

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes — Thanksgiving Bounce
items.title: The Fed is 'the uncomfortable guest': credit is holding, but nobody has given the market a reason to chase
items.idea: A December hike remains the main headwind. The S&P is threatening to match one of its choppiest stretches since the 2022 bear market. Credit has held up well enough that equity vol hasn't become a broader financial problem. Innes's line: the market has found a reason to stop selling, not a reason to start chasing.
items.angle: Credit holding is key. If IG/HY spreads stay calm through the hike, this is an equity-only correction. Compare with the Asian GPU lenders below, where credit is not holding.
items.tweetA: IG spreads are calm while the Nasdaq makes 4% intraday swings. Equity vol without credit stress has historically been a buyable correction. The exception: 15.5% GPU term loans in Asia. Watch the AI credit niche, not the HY index.
items.tweetB: 'A reason to stop selling, not a reason to start chasing.' That's what you get from a December hike priced, CTA exposure near zero, and no new catalyst. Expect a range, not a V.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (whatsthelatest.ai)
items.title: UK net migration more than halves to 77,000, the lowest since 1997 outside the pandemic
items.idea: In the year to June 2026, UK net migration fell to 77,000, less than half the prior year and the lowest annual level since 1997 excluding pandemic years. The fall was mostly from fewer non-EU arrivals. The piece argues this gives Labour room to defend the EU youth mobility deal reached on Nov 20, though first-year flows under the new route will distort the balance.
items.angle: UK labour supply growth is collapsing at the same time as the UK has a services-heavy, labour-intensive economy. That's wage-sticky for BoE and bad for the potential growth assumption in gilt pricing.
items.tweetA: UK net migration: from roughly 900k at peak to 77k. That's a labour supply shock most growth models haven't caught up with. Expect services inflation to stay sticky and the BoE to sound more hawkish than the growth data says it should. $GBP
items.tweetB: Britain has cut net migration by more than 90% from peak without anyone calling it a policy win, because the fall came from non-EU visas while the government is now opening a new EU youth route. Policy is pulling in two directions at once.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (whatsthelatest.ai)
items.title: UK 'cutting costs bill' gives ministers a vehicle to implement future EU deals, with the single market and customs union carved out
items.idea: The government introduced a bill that lets ministers implement some future agreements with Brussels by secondary process, explicitly excluding re-entry to the single market, customs union or EU. The Nov 20 reset covered food trade (SPS) and youth mobility, with tuition fees unresolved. Burnham wants a quick fee deal.
items.angle: This is the legal plumbing for incremental re-alignment. Watch SPS and food trade first: UK food importers, ports and grocers are the direct beneficiaries.
items.tweetA: Brexit reversal isn't happening by referendum. It's happening by enabling bill: a legal channel for implementing EU agreements one sector at a time, with the three politically toxic words carved out. Watch UK food importers and grocers. $TSCO
items.tweetB: Just as interesting is who is negotiating: Burnham is pushing on tuition fees. The youth mobility deal may end up being priced by how much a year at a Spanish university costs a kid from Manchester.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (whatsthelatest.ai)
items.title: Pablo Hernández de Cos chosen to succeed Lagarde as ECB president
items.idea: The former Bank of Spain governor (and later BIS general manager) secured support from the EU's largest countries to succeed Christine Lagarde as ECB president.
items.angle: A southern-European, BIS-trained, financial-stability-focused president. Expect a focus on bank supervision and fragmentation tools, which matters for BTP-Bund and periphery spreads.
items.tweetA: First Spaniard to run the ECB, and he comes from the BIS, the central bank of central banks. A banking-stability technocrat replacing a lawyer-politician. The periphery spread trade just got a sympathetic referee. $EWP $EWI
items.tweetB: The Fed is hiking in December. The ECB's next president came up through Spanish bank supervision after the 2012 crisis. If the policy gap widens, EUR/USD will reflect how far Hernández de Cos is willing to diverge.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (whatsthelatest.ai)
items.title: Nvidia freezes chip orders for buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia
items.idea: Per Semafor (via The Pressure Point's 'Things happen'), Nvidia froze chip orders for buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as Washington restricts China's access to US compute. This is the supply-side counterpart of the Asian neocloud stress described in the Rewiring piece.
items.angle: Southeast Asia was the offshore conduit for Chinese compute. Freezing orders there is a channel check on how much of Nvidia's 'sovereign/APAC' demand was really China.
items.tweetA: Nvidia froze orders to 4 SEA countries, the same 4 that host most of China's offshore compute. If you want to know how much 'Malaysia demand' was really ByteDance demand, this is how you find out. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Two headlines, one story: Nvidia freezes SEA chip orders, and SEA GPU rental listings double in four weeks. The offshore China compute trade is unwinding from both the supply and the demand side at once.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (whatsthelatest.ai)
items.title: North Korea reportedly halts missile and shell shipments to Russia over Moscow's outreach to Seoul
items.idea: Ukrainian military intelligence says North Korea temporarily halted missile and artillery shell shipments to Russia after a dispute over Moscow's outreach to South Korea.
items.angle: If confirmed, Russia loses a key munitions supplier at the margin. That bears on the Ukraine front line and on Moscow's incentive to negotiate, which feeds through to European gas and defence names.
items.tweetA: Pyongyang has supplied a large share of Russia's artillery shells. If it's cutting Moscow off because Putin is talking to Seoul, the Russia–DPRK axis is more transactional than it looked. Bad for Russia's shell budget, interesting for European defence demand.
items.tweetB: Moscow courting Seoul is the bigger story. Russia wants Korean industrial capacity (shipbuilding, chips, autos) more than North Korean shells. Pyongyang just found out where it ranks.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (whatsthelatest.ai)
items.title: Trump calls pre-midterm GDP figures fake and demands an investigation
items.idea: President Trump called the GDP figures released before the midterms fake and demanded an investigation (Al Jazeera, via The Pressure Point).
items.angle: An attack on statistical agencies is a slow-burn term premium story: if markets doubt official data, they demand compensation and shift weight to private alternatives.
items.tweetA: When the President calls the GDP print fake, the market's response is to trust it less. That shows up in term premium and in demand for alternative data, from ADP to Truflation. Data credibility is a priced variable now.
items.tweetB: First BLS, now GDP. Each attack on official statistics makes private data vendors more valuable and the Treasury curve a little less anchored. Nobody models the cost of a doubted data release.

items.source: The Pressure Point / Michael McDonough (whatsthelatest.ai)
items.title: Thanksgiving storms knock out power to more than 600,000 US homes and businesses
items.idea: Thanksgiving storms disrupted US holiday travel and left more than 600,000 homes and businesses without power (Euronews).
items.angle: Another data point for grid hardening and distribution capex, the less glamorous side of the power trade next to AI data-center load.
items.tweetA: 600k without power on Thanksgiving. The grid conversation is all about data centres, but the distribution grid is still failing at the first serious storm. Utilities' hardening capex has a long way to run. $XLU
items.tweetB: Data-centre load growth plus a distribution network that fails in every storm. Regulators can approve both, but ratepayers pay for both. Keep an eye on residential electricity prices going into 2027.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes — China's Orphaned GPUs
items.title: B300 rental price rolls over: $7.72 → $7.19/GPU-hr in a month, after running up from $4.55
items.idea: Nvidia B300 capacity rented at ~$7.72/GPU-hr at end-October and $7.19 by Tuesday (≈-7%), after climbing from ~$4.55 over the preceding year. Innes notes prices had begun turning before the new US export rules; the rules added a fresh supply shock to a market already losing momentum.
items.angle: GPU-hour pricing is the closest thing to a spot price for AI compute. A rollover in the newest generation is a key signal for neocloud ($CRWV, $NBIS) unit economics.
items.tweetA: B300s went from $4.55 to $7.72 an hour, and now $7.19. Newest-gen GPU rents falling 7% in a month, during a 'compute shortage'. The shortage turned out to be regional, and the price is starting to show it. $CRWV $NBIS
items.tweetB: Quick math: a B300 at $7.19/hr, fully utilised, earns about $63k a year. At $4.75 on a 3-year deal it's about $41.6k. That 34% gap is the difference between a neocloud that services its debt and one that doesn't.

charts.desc: Five images in email; likely B300 rental price curve ($4.55 → $7.72 → $7.19). 🔥 Price-curve chart worth saving

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes — China's Orphaned GPUs
items.title: China's offshore compute: 0.5–0.75 GW of ASEAN demand, and a quarter of Malaysia's pipeline
items.idea: China-linked AI workloads are estimated at ~0.5–0.75 GW of IT demand, or 15–25% of operational ASEAN data-centre demand. Separately, ~3.8 GW of Malaysia's development pipeline (roughly a quarter of planned capacity) is associated with Chinese operators. New US rules add licensing for advanced chips to several SEA countries and restrict remote access by Chinese firms, with a 90-day compliance window from Nov 19 (≈ Feb 17).
items.angle: Johor's data-centre boom was partly a China workaround. Malaysian DC REITs, utilities (TNB) and contractors face a demand hole that US hyperscalers may only partly fill.
items.tweetA: A quarter of Malaysia's data-centre pipeline was built for Chinese tenants. The US just gave them 90 days to comply: Feb 17. Johor's DC boom now depends on how quickly US hyperscalers will sign up to replace them.
items.tweetB: The export-control story has always been about chips. This is about real estate: 3.8 GW of Malaysian shells, substations and fibre whose anchor tenant may need a licence it won't get. Power and land don't move to a new country.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes — China's Orphaned GPUs
items.title: Customer concentration: Nscale 73% of revenue from ByteDance, DayOne 69% from its top customer
items.idea: Norway's Nscale reportedly generated 73% of 2025 revenue from one customer identified as ByteDance; DayOne's largest customer was ~69% of 2025 revenue. Financing across Malaysia and Singapore has leaned heavily on ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent contracts.
items.angle: Single-tenant concentration plus export-licence dependency is the textbook setup for a covenant event. Check for similar concentration in listed neoclouds' 10-Ks.
items.tweetA: 73% of Nscale's revenue came from one customer, and that customer now needs a US export licence to keep using the chips. That's no longer counterparty risk. It's regulatory risk on top of counterparty risk.
items.tweetB: Every neocloud deck shows 'contracted backlog'. Read it next to the customer list. When 70% of backlog depends on one Chinese tenant and one Washington licence, the backlog figure tells you very little.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes — China's Orphaned GPUs
items.title: GPU marketplace flips: listings 9,100 → 18,000, buyer enquiries 18,600 → 8,500 in four weeks
items.idea: Over four weeks to Nov 20, third-party GPUs offered roughly doubled (9,100 → 18,000) while buyer enquiries fell by more than half (18,600 → 8,500). Capacity offered on >1-year terms more than tripled. A B300 was ~$6.85/hr on 12 months vs ~$4.75 on 3 years. Sellers want 36-48 month terms with prepayments; buyers want ≤1 year with little cash upfront.
items.angle: The supply/demand ratio went from ~0.5x to ~2.1x in a month. Even in a small sample, a move that size is a regime signal for compute spot pricing.
items.tweetA: Four weeks ago there were 2 GPU buyers for every listing. Now there are 2 listings for every buyer. A 4x swing in the supply/demand ratio in one month, in the 'scarcest asset in the world'.
items.tweetB: The real spread in AI compute isn't price, it's tenor. Sellers need 36-48 months to satisfy their banks. Buyers will only commit to 12. Whoever has the balance sheet to bridge that gap (hyperscalers) gets Blackwell at a 30% discount. $MSFT $META

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes — China's Orphaned GPUs
items.title: Asian GPU credit tightens: 16 of 23 term-loan requests rejected, 15.5% rates, LTV down to 50-60%
items.idea: In a sample of GPU financing activity, lenders passed on 16 of 23 term-loan requests. Indicative term-loan rates were ~15.5% and bridge financing approached 20%. Loan-to-value fell to ~50–60% from 70–80% in the summer. Some China-intended equipment is reportedly being offered for outright sale, adding secondary supply that pressures collateral values.
items.angle: This is the AI-capex credit cycle starting to turn in its most leveraged niche. LTV going from 75% to 55% while collateral prices fall is a classic margin spiral.
items.tweetA: 70% rejection rate on GPU term loans. 15.5% coupons. LTV cut from 75% to 55% in one season. That's what a credit cycle turning looks like in the most leveraged corner of AI, while the IG index looks calm.
items.tweetB: The math on a 55% LTV GPU loan at 15.5%: the equity has to cover nearly half the box, and rents are falling 7% a month. Distressed GPU sales will show up first in secondary hardware prices, before they show up in any credit index.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes — China's Orphaned GPUs
items.title: APAC data-centre lending: from ~zero in 2023 to $49B+, with specific deals now under review
items.idea: APAC data-centre lending grew from virtually nothing in 2023 to more than $49B. Deals under scrutiny include an expanded $6.6B financing for Bridge Data Centres (Malaysia), a $480M GPU facility for Aolani Cloud and a $372M loan involving Digital Halo. At least one private lender reportedly declined a $300M financing for Thailand's GMI Cloud, whose capacity was meant for Tencent.
items.angle: $49B built in under three years, underwritten against Chinese tenant cash flows. Watch SEA banks' (Maybank, CIMB, DBS, OCBC) DC exposure disclosures in Q4 results.
items.tweetA: APAC data-centre debt went from ~$0 to $49B in three years. Most of it was underwritten in a world where ByteDance could rent B300s in Johor. That world ended Nov 19. $DBSDY
items.tweetB: The line I keep coming back to: 'The customers can move. The debt stays behind.' That's the summary of every overbuild: railways, telecom fibre, Chinese property. The hardware may find new tenants. The loans were sized for the old ones.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Stephen Innes — China's Orphaned GPUs
items.title: Benign read: stranded Blackwell capacity becomes a discount for US/EU buyers
items.idea: Innes's counterpoint: demand for advanced compute hasn't collapsed, and installed, operational Blackwell capacity may become available to US/EU firms at discounts to the original China-tenant terms. The pain falls on the Asian operators and lenders who borrowed against those contracts, not on the AI cycle overall. Washington licensing decisions in the next three months could ease or deepen the stress.
items.angle: The winners are compute buyers with balance sheets: AI labs and hyperscalers renting instead of building. The losers are leveraged middlemen.
items.tweetA: Oddly, the China export rules may be the best thing to happen to US AI startups' compute budgets this year: installed Blackwell, already powered, at a 30% discount, because the original tenant isn't allowed to use it.
items.tweetB: Aggregate scarcity and local glut can coexist. AI compute is scarce globally and oversupplied in Johor. The arbitrage is latency-tolerant workloads like training and batch inference moving to wherever the stranded GPUs are.
